reasoning: A ties nearly every claim to an evidence ID. Its pixel and layout claims check out against the screenshots. It labels motion findings [O] or [H] honestly and explains why mobile changes happen: trading time for space, preparing separate assets per width, and reordering content for reading. The patterns and principles are grounded in evidence that repeats across the page. It respects scope by giving an implementation handoff instead of code. B is a thin 5-point summary. It leaks process notes (a subagent was blocked; it cites a process-log.md that is not in the folder). Its motion claims, such as the glow direction changing, can't be checked. It also built a full index.html, which the user said research should not do. A is long and dense, but it is far more trustworthy.
a_strengths: Clear evidence IDs (S-/P-/I-/H-/X-) with an [O]/[I]/[H] split
Motion table is honest: only two items reach [O] (subtitle rotation, logo marquee); the rest stay hypotheses, each with a way to verify
Mobile analysis explains the reasoning behind each change (time for space, per-width assets, triangle scaling less than the viewport)
Patterns cite evidence that repeats; principles trace back to those patterns
Implementation handoff summary instead of building a page; flags uncertain items so they are not copied as spec
Notes conflicts between sources (branding primary blue vs what the screenshots show)
a_weaknesses: Very long and dense; the 'evidence level' label system adds reading load
Cites tablet.png and mobile-wait6s.png, which are not in the delivered folder, so the tablet-only claims and the I-01 time comparison can't be checked here
Some overlap between §4 and the VP patterns

Admits that durations, easing and breakpoints were not measured
